target_customer: Restaurants and small neighborhood food retailers in Latin America
problem: Small restaurants buy fresh produce and supplies through fragmented, unreliable wholesale channels. Frubana sourced fruit and vegetables directly from farms and delivered them, later adding more categories and credit.
business_model: B2B marketplace and distribution with product margin, plus credit for retailers
product_category: B2B food supply e-commerce and logistics

founders.name: Fabian Gomez Gutierrez
prior_employers: Rappi (oversaw expansion in Barranquilla, Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro)
founders.background_notes: Colombian; named an Endeavor entrepreneur by Endeavor Colombia in February 2023 (Bloomberg Linea). Prior employer from the NeoFeed article.

exit.reason: Last delivery July 30, 2025 in Brazil after a planned new investment of about 40 million dollars reportedly did not materialize; earlier closures in Colombia and Mexico (Feb 2024) were blamed on macroeconomic conditions blocking fundraising

technical_complexity.rationale: Marketplace software is standard, but running sourcing, cold chain, routing and delivery across several countries adds hard operational and logistics engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Direct farm sourcing and delivery density could create cost advantages, but the model needs heavy capital and margins are thin, and none of the sources describe a lock in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying the model; the company ended on funding and demand problems.

market_need_then: Brazil alone has more than 2.5 million small restaurants and food businesses sourcing produce, with small farms producing 77 percent of agricultural output (search summary of a Brazilian press source), a fragmented supply chain that attracted large venture funding.

branding.community_and_virality: Covered widely in Latin American business press (Forbes Brasil 2021, Bloomberg Linea, Contxto, NeoFeed), mostly for funding and shutdown rather than brand.

brand_strength.rationale: Recognized in Latin American startup press and across three countries, but no source describes brand assets, community or consumer pull, and the closure news is the main later coverage.

pivots.from: Fruit and vegetable B2B sourced directly from farms (YC application summary)
pivots.to: Everything store for restaurants including credit for retailers
pivots.why: Broadened categories and added credit via an Accion and Mastercard partnership; the date of the change is not stated

outcome_analysis: Frubana raised a 25 million Series A in April 2020, 65 million Series B in June 2021 and a reported 75 million Series C led by DST Global in July 2022, for about 271 million in seven rounds per NeoFeed. High rates and food inflation hit it in 2023, it closed Colombia and Mexico in February 2024, then Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Campinas, and made its last Brazilian delivery on July 30, 2025 after a planned 40 million dollar raise failed. An anonymous former employee also blamed mismanagement and labor suits, which is not corroborated.
notes: The company site was not fetched separately; the YC page and press were used. Conflicts: aggregators report a 94 million dollar Series C in November 2021 led by DST Global (another says 80 million), while NeoFeed dates a 75 million dollar Series C to July 2022; this is unresolved and the NeoFeed figure is recorded. Total raised is 271 million across seven rounds (NeoFeed, El Colombiano) or 331 million (PitchBook), so recorded rounds (about 165 million) leave a gap; the seed and other rounds were not found. PitchBook lists a 2023 deal with Zak as an acquisition, found in one source only and not recorded. Series A date is January per one source and April 2020 per LatAmList. Competitors: Cayena and Raizs appeared only in undated or later articles, so the list is empty. The 40 million dollar failed raise comes from one NeoFeed report quoting anonymous staff.
